003d08dc-6215-5320-a8d3-88161baeb779.title: Explore Baroque
003d08dc-6215-5320-a8d3-88161baeb779.description: In the Baroque era, splendour became the dominant principle of European art In the Baroque era, splendour became the dominant principle of European art and as a consequence there was an incredibly rich explosion of the arts. The nobility and the church constantly tried to outdo each other in displaying the reign of earthly or heavenly powers while the rising bourgeoisie wished to demonstrate its new status. Well-known masterpieces and hidden treasures invite you to explore the exuberance of Baroque art and architecture and their cultural environment.

country_texts.text:
The Counter-Reformation brought forward a veritable boom in Austrian construction. New ‘houses of God’ were erected everywhere as a sign of a re-strengthened Christianity. Numerous new churches and monasteries emerged with magnificent fresco cycles, but Gothic churches were also commonly furnished with Baroque paintings. This animated, expressive style had its origins in Italy, where it blossomed into a luxuriant display of splendour and emotion. Stucco works are essential decorative elements, which were produced mainly by southern German artists (namely from Wessobrunn), from fruit garlands in the early Baroque to graceful rocailles during the late Baroque period. Frescoes range from small colourful pieces to huge pastose designs spanning across vaults as with illusionistic motifs.  
  
Gardens along with the connected castle now represent so-called *Gesamtkunstwerke* (total works of art), and the newly developed medium of the opera shows refined stage machinery ranging from water arts and horse ballets to fireworks. The largest palace in Tyrol, the imperial Hofburg, was refashioned in the late Baroque style and termed by Maria Theresa as the “little Schönbrunn of the Alps”. The most notable monasteries of the region, Wilten & Stams, were refurbished into Baroque.

Southern Bavaria unites the southern parts of Upper Bavaria and Lower Swabia. In the Baroque era, these regions were the scene of some intense building activity – so much that even today the monuments from this time make their mark on the landscape. Not only are there many splendorous monasteries and palaces with rich furnishings, but everywhere one finds the onion-shaped spires of village churches built or rebuilt in Baroque style, typical of the countryside. Over the course of the 18th century the gracious and elegant French styles of Régence and Rococo, originating from profane noble or courtly buildings, came to influence Southern German ecclesiastical architecture, leading to those miracles dubbed ‘Rococo churches’. A typical feature of Rococo style is the popular, enchanting, friendly, indeed sometimes childishly naive character of the painted and sculpted depictions, often enriched with a touch of humour – one needs only to look at the countless playful small angels found in so many churches to find such flourishes.

The appearance of Baroque in Croatia coincided with the cessation of the Ottoman invasion at the beginning of the 17th century and simultaneous ecclesiastical renewal after the Council of Trent. Perhaps to a greater extent than in other European countries, Baroque in Croatia manifests the duality of stylistic influences of the Central European and Mediterranean cultural and artistic circles. It is a consequence of the historical integration of the two central Croatian regions – continental Croatia and coastal Croatia – into two dominant political and cultural options of the 17th and 18th centuries: the Habsburg Monarchy and the Venetian Republic. That general dichotomy has its exceptions: the expansion of the Central European cultural circle on the Croatian coast and Habsburg estates in Istria and Kvarner, as well as the phenomenon of the Republic of Dubrovnik, a free city-state in south-eastern Croatia, oriented towards Rome and southern Italy. The most prominent clients in both regions – Jesuits, Franciscans, dioceses and nobility – turn mainly to foreign architects, sculptors and painters, but also to notable domestic authors who had their workshops in larger towns. During both Baroque centuries, we can trace two simultaneous phenomena - an increase in artistic standards, promoted by works of foreign masters and educated domestic artists, and a provincial variant of Baroque in the creations of local authors. Particularly in sculpture and painting the first category combines quality artworks of various provenances, and the second includes works of often reproductive character. Nevertheless, they both fit perfectly into the narrative of the Baroque in the vast area of its spread.

The Ottoman occupation of the middle part of Hungary from the 1540s cut short, stopped or altered the continuity of arts and architecture influenced by Western European ideas. However, the Baroque arrived in the early 17th century to those parts that were not occupied by the Turks (North and a part of West Hungary) as can be seen in the compelling Baroque rebuilding of Sopron after a devastating fire in 1676. The new style and its accompanying ideals would spread across the whole of the country gradually after the reconquering wars at the end of the 17th century. These circumstances led to entire Baroque cityscapes built over empty sites or atop cities destroyed in war like Buda, Győr or Eger. The nobility was eager to commission country and town palaces in the new style with gardens built following the Baroque schemes and the emerging bourgeoisie also erected their town home following the ideas of the Baroque. Among the main promoters was the Catholic Church, mainly the Jesuit order. Grandiose churches and colleges were built to serve new demands to show rich decorations and the perspective and theatrical effects that were already used in the Western part of Europe. On city squares, Baroque statues were erected to glorify the Christian Faith and Religion or to commemorate important events. Alongside the activities of foreign artists and architects (mainly from Italy or German-speaking countries) in Hungary, local masters also took over the new fashion. From the middle of the 18th century arrived the fashion of the Rococo and a Neoclassical Late-Baroque as well.

By the early 17th century, the arts of the Baroque began to flourish in papal Rome, thanks to the contribution of artists such as Caravaggio and Bernini, Lanfranco, Pietro da Cortona and Borromini. Popes and cardinals promoted a majestic and emotional art celebrating the power of the Roman Catholic Church by means of public undertakings: piazzas, bridges, fountains, churches, altarpieces, chapels, all characterized by grandiose architectures, dynamic spaces, flowing curves, rich colours and luxurious materials. Noble families competed with the popes in commissioning outstanding palaces and villas, as well as frescoes, paintings and statues often depicting profane mythological subjects. Not only Rome but also its environs witnessed the spread of the splendour of the Baroque art: for example Frascati, Grottaferrata and Castel Gandolfo, where the popes and their families had villas and gardens built. Bologna was the other important city of the Papal State: cradle of the naturalism of the Carracci, Bologna shows a peculiar declination of the Baroque language, more classical and restrained, through its noble palaces, churches, villas and theatres within the city and in its surroundings.

Portuguese monuments collection aims to introduce the visitor to the extremely rich variety of Baroque heritage in Portugal. Taking advantage of the financial resources provided by Brazilian gold shipments from 1695 till the second half of the 18th century, King João V, as well as mainly the religious orders and the aristocracy were enabled to commission a wide array of civil, military and religious monumental ensembles and artistic masterpieces, displayed throughout the whole country, from Minho to Algarve, Madeira and Azores.  
In addition to exhibiting the splendour of both royal and religious power, these works of art convey the peculiar Portuguese interpretation of Baroque that blends the ‘exoticism’ of its culture, originated by the encounter with other civilizations from Brazil to the Far East, together with the richness of its typical artistic language, whose main features are the gilded wood and the *azulejos* panels.

01ee875c-c376-5883-bea9-b652d274bb33.title: The Umayyads and their Christian Subjects
01ee875c-c376-5883-bea9-b652d274bb33.description:
The 6th and early 1st/7th centuries were filled with a remarkable upsurge in the construc­tion of churches in Jordan. Most of these churches survived remarkably well the military campaigns of the around 10/630's, which brought the Arab-Muslims into Syria. Archaeological research in the last 15 years has shown that no less than 56 churches in Jordan continue to be used well until the f. h. 2nd/mid-8th entury and after, and no fewer than eight churches were built or repaved with coloured mosaics in the Umayyad period (41/661-132/750).  
  
One factor making for continuity was Christian city, which was the singular and important element in maintaining the cohesion and solidarity of the inhabitants of towns and villages. Each community preserved its own laws and customs as well as keeping its leaders.

0234880b-5c93-5316-a337-8a874f90c139.title: The Pilgrimage Road between Jerusalem and Hebron
0234880b-5c93-5316-a337-8a874f90c139.description:
Throughout the ages, Jerusalem and Hebron have been interconnected as a result of their religious, political, social and scientific interaction, and for being generally under the same administrative system. In the Ayyubid period, the post of Inspector to the two holy *haram*s of Jerusalem and Hebron was appointed, emulating the post in Mecca and Medina. Having developed during the Mamluk period, this position became an integral and highly respected religious post.  
  
This itinerary will follow the mountainous road that stretches for a disance of 40 km. and connects Jerusalem to Hebron. Many pilgrims have taken this road since time immemorial, as did the *caliphs* and sultans who visited these holy sites, and all the trade caravans on their way from Syria to Egypt and vice versa.  
  
On our way from Jerusalem to Hebron we will visit some of the sites that played a vital role in shaping the Islamic history of Palestine.

031a8efe-b569-559c-b989-57c3d06db8e2.title: Royal Art in the Norman Age: Institutional Architecture
031a8efe-b569-559c-b989-57c3d06db8e2.description:
Interpretations of the great works of the Norman period produced in Sicily between the 9th and 10th centuries are extremely articulate. Introduction of elements of Arabic art during the effective period of enforced Islamisation of Sicily had been preceded with a long series of exchanges (and of clashes) with the cultures of the island's populations; in architecture, Islamic art which at that time availed itself of Greco-Roman and Persian influences, had found a strong Byzantine presence with significant elements of earlier times.  
  
After an initial period of permanence in the regulations and in the artistic ways in the respective areas of cultural origin, whether the Norman Dynasty or the senior Siculo-Greek dignitaries of the new Kingdom of Sicily jointly promoted the artistic, scientific and cultural blossoming already initiated in Sicily (from 969) by the same Fatimids, giving birth to the richest artistic development of the age, characterised by the autonomous Siculo-Norman decline in a now mature Islamic *Koine.*

03f23c73-2f9d-5036-8bdb-fb64a80dfc17.title: The Lock of the Sea
03f23c73-2f9d-5036-8bdb-fb64a80dfc17.description: For many centuries, the Çanakkale and Istanbul (Bosphorus) Straits have been a major source of conflict between nations. At the beginning of the 14th century, the Anatolian shores of the Strait were under the sovereignty of the Karasi Emirate. When the Ottomans destroyed the Karasi Emirate around the middle of 14th century, they gained control over the shores of the area. At the same time, the Ottomans gained a base in Gelibolu, on the other side of the Çanakkale Strait in return for helping John VI Cantacuzenus, who at the time was struggling to acquire the Byzantine throne (1354). From this date on the Ottomans rapidly acquired all of Thrace. Gelibolu became a much-frequented place for people passing from Anatolia to Thrace. Built on the Gelibolu-Edirne route, Uzunköprü, literally the Long Bridge, is one of the longest bridges of Thrace. This bridge indicates the importance given to the trade and conquest routes that tied Anatolia and Europe together in the first half of 15th century.

06373f8f-cb0e-5013-97ed-7a0ea76e58fc.title: TAFESSERA
06373f8f-cb0e-5013-97ed-7a0ea76e58fc.description:
A village in the Beni Snous Valley, Tafessera is one of the oldest settlements in the region. Around the very old medina, which has kept its earliest Berber structures, traces of the Roman Empire in vestiges of the chapel of Kouiyet Errom Fortress have been dated to the time of St. Augustine (AD 354–430).  
  
Kouiyet Errom, literally small Christian fort, is today the main mosque of the village. The walls surrounding it make a strong first impression. It attracts numerous visitors and the curious from the entire region, as does the *madrasa* (theological school).  
  
Apart from an old spring, now dry but still the subject of an ancient cult, the uniqueness of the village lies in the prehistoric underground caves that date back millennia. The composition of rocks in the region, mainly karst limestone, contributed to the formation of underground corridors, caves, fissures and natural grottos that provided Tafessera, like other villages in the valley, with hidden natural dwelling places and numerous tunnels leading to other villages.

extra.author: Author: Curatorial committee (Farida Benouis, Houria Chérid, Lakhdar Drias, Amine Semar)   Translation: Judy Harter (French to English)

06e8335d-8fa7-5962-ba1c-393323f80132.title: MIRANDA DO DOURO
06e8335d-8fa7-5962-ba1c-393323f80132.description:
The history of Miranda do Douro goes back to the time of the first King D. Afonso Henriques, who set up an enclosure of shelters to encourage settlers, in a harsh, remote area where there was only a small hamlet. There was little success at first and it was only in the time of D. Dinis, in 1286, that the settlement was raised to town status. Its position on the frontier with the neighbouring kingdom encouraged trade and local craftsmanship and eventually the town was made the see of the diocese in 1545.  
  
The Manueline era, a time of peaceful association with Castile, was one of great prosperity and a large number of both Portuguese and Spanish Jews, converted or not, settled here. New houses and churches were built, as well as public buildings, such as the Customs House, and naturally the defences were completely overhauled and renovated. This led to a polarisation between Miranda and Bragança and a healthy dispute between primacies, privileges and development. A large part of the city’s Manueline heritage disappeared with the explosion of the gun powder store at the Castle on 8th May 1762.
